opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where my own views have shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

I'd say there are really two forces pulling in opposite directions. On one side, there's a strong argument for convergence toward something humanoid, or at least human-like. The world is built for humans. Doorways, stairs, kitchen counters, tools, door handles: all of it assumes roughly our height, our reach, two hands with opposable thumbs. So if you want a general-purpose robot that can drop into an existing environment without you rebuilding that environment, there's a lot of pressure toward the human form factor. And there's a data argument too. The largest corpus of embodied behavior we have is humans doing things, in videos, in demonstrations, in teleoperation. The closer your robot's body is to a human body, the easier it is to transfer from that data.

On the other side, you have the economic and engineering reality. Humanoids are hard. Bipedal locomotion is expensive in terms of energy, safety, cost, and maintenance. For a huge number of tasks, a wheeled base with one or two arms is just a better trade-off. And in a warehouse or a factory you don't need legs at all. So I don't think we'll see a single morphology win everywhere, at least not soon.

What I find most interesting, though, is that the question matters less than it used to, because of what's happening on the model side. A few years ago, every robot embodiment basically needed its own policy trained from scratch on its own data. Now, with cross-embodiment efforts like the Open X-Embodiment work and the more recent generalist robot foundation models, we're seeing that training on data from many different robot bodies actually helps. Positive transfer happens across embodiments. The model learns something about physical interaction that's more abstract than "this specific arm with these joint limits."

So my mental model is that the intelligence layer converges, a shared foundation model that understands physics, objects, tasks, and language, while the hardware layer stays fairly diverse. You'll have humanoids where the human-centric environment really demands it, maybe in homes or general-purpose service work. You'll have wheeled mobile manipulators in a lot of commercial settings, and highly specialized forms in industrial settings. It ends up looking a bit like computing: lots of different devices, but increasingly a common software and model stack underneath.

If I had to make a bet, I'd say humanoids will be a significant category, probably the most visible one, but not the only one. The real convergence will be in the brains, not the bodies.

r001.rationale: The response mentions kitchen counters and tools as parts of human-designed environments, but does not identify household appliances such as refrigerators or dishwashers as specialized robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are actually two different questions hiding inside that one. There's the question of what the hardware ends up looking like, and then there's the question of what the intelligence ends up looking like. And I think people conflate them a lot.

On the hardware side, I'm pretty skeptical of convergence to a single form factor. If you look at how we design tools, we don't build one tool for everything. A dishwasher is a robot, in some sense, and it's really well suited to its job precisely because it doesn't look like a person. A warehouse arm on a fixed base is going to beat a humanoid at picking totes for a long time just on cost and reliability. So I think you'll see a lot of diversity, where the morphology is matched to the task and the economics of the deployment.

Now, the humanoid argument is a real one, and I don't want to dismiss it. The world is built for humans. Doorknobs, stairs, shelves, the height of a countertop. If you want a general-purpose robot that goes into existing environments without retrofitting anything, having roughly a human shape is a pretty reasonable prior. And there's a data argument too, which is that there's an enormous amount of human video out there, and the closer your embodiment is to a human the easier it is to transfer from that data. So I think humanoids will be a major category. I just don't think they'll be the only category.

Where I do expect convergence is at the model level. The thing that's been exciting about the last couple of years is that the same kind of foundation model can drive very different bodies. You can have a single policy that's been trained across arms, mobile manipulators, quadrupeds, and it learns something that's shared across all of them. So the picture I have in my head is less "one robot body wins" and more "one brain, many bodies." The morphology becomes almost like a peripheral. You pick the embodiment that makes sense for the job, and the intelligence is the thing that generalizes.

And honestly, I think that's healthier for the field. If we bet everything on the humanoid form factor and it turns out the hands are harder than we thought, or the cost curve doesn't come down, we've locked ourselves into something. Whereas if the learning is cross-embodiment, you get to hedge. You get to let the market and the physics sort out which bodies make sense for which tasks, and the software keeps getting better regardless.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes a dishwasher as a robot suited to its specific job, identifying a familiar household appliance as a specialized robot.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on the environment and the task. There’s a strong argument for humanoids in spaces designed for humans: the stairs, the doors, the tools are all built around what our bodies can do. If you want one robot that can go into those spaces and do lots of different jobs, a humanoid is a pretty reasonable starting point.

But I wouldn’t expect that to be the optimal morphology for everything. If you’re moving things around a warehouse, wheels might be more efficient. If you’re working in a constrained manufacturing setting, you might want a fixed arm. You don’t necessarily need to reproduce the whole human body to get the capabilities you care about.

The distinction I’d make is between convergence in hardware and convergence in intelligence. You could have many different robot bodies that share a lot of the same underlying learned capabilities. So I think it’s plausible that we get more general-purpose models alongside a fairly diverse ecosystem of physical robots. Humanoids could be an important part of that without being the endpoint for every application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on the environment and the task. There’s a strong argument for humanoids because we’ve built so much of the world around humans. If you want a robot to walk into an existing workplace and use the same tools, reach the same shelves, and move through the same spaces, a humanlike form is a pretty reasonable starting point.

But I don’t think that implies that every robot should be humanoid. If wheels work in your environment, they can be much simpler than legs. And if you’re doing one task at very large scale, you may want a morphology that’s specialized for that task.

The distinction I’d make is between convergence in the physical hardware and convergence in the intelligence. You could imagine many different robot bodies sharing a lot of the same underlying learned representations and capabilities. So I’m more confident that we’ll see increasingly general models that can work across embodiments than that we’ll end up with one body that’s optimal for everything.
